summary: An April 1st joke RFC that proposes a TCP option to denote packet mood. It is humorous, not a real protocol, and is published for informational purposes.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine every message carrying a little face showing how it feels, happy or grumpy. It is a joke document.

questions: what is the tcp mood option
subtitle: An April 1st joke about tagging network packets with emoticons.

tldr.problem: This is an April 1st joke RFC. It humorously proposes that network packets should express emotions via emoticon emoticons, reflecting the mood of the sending system or user.
tldr.mechanism: Add a new TCP option (option 25) that carries 2 to 3 ASCII characters encoding common emoticons like :) for happy, :( for sad, or :@  for frustrated.
tldr.outcome: This is satire. The RFC was never intended for implementation. It is published as humor, though the technical descriptions of emoticon encoding are accurate.

today: RFC 5841 is an Informational, April 1st RFC and was never intended for deployment. It is a humorous thought experiment about packet behavior. The TCP mood option was never adopted, and no implementations exist.

sections.title: Packet Mood
sections.content: This April 1st RFC proposes a TCP option to express "packet mood." Packets cannot actually feel emotions, but the RFC humorously suggests that the network behavior and context can imply an emotional state: a packet that succeeds is happy, one that gets dropped many times is sad or angry, and so on. The proposal uses ASCII emoticons to encode these moods inside the TCP header.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a joke. But if packets could feel, which ones would be happy or grumpy? The RFC answers that question.

sections.title: Emoticon Encoding
sections.content: The RFC defines option 25 in the TCP header with a length of 4 or 5 bytes. Each mood is encoded as 2 or 3 ASCII characters. For example, :) is a happy packet (bytes 0x3A, 0x29), :D is amused, and >:@ is angry. Multiple mood options can appear in one header to express complex emotions. The RFC specifies 12 moods and includes an ABNF syntax for how they would be encoded.
sections.plainLanguage: The emoticon is just two or three characters, like a tiny smiley face, tucked into the packet header.

sections.title: Example Moods and Use Cases
sections.content: The RFC proposes specific rules for when to use each mood. Happy packets have low latency and no retransmissions. Sad packets are in sessions with very high packet loss (over 20% retransmission rate). Angry packets are retransmitted. Frustrated packets are retransmitted multiple times. Confused packets arrive out of order. Bored packets carry accounting data or RFCs. Amused packets contain jokes. The RFC even suggests silly packets for playful interchanges and evil packets for destructive activity.
sections.plainLanguage: Different situations get different moods: a smooth conversation is happy, but a broken connection is frustrated.
